Tennessee law sets out when a person occupying land can claim title by adverse possession, and how an owner can remove someone who has no right to be there.

What the official sources say

  • Under the statutory forms, seven years' adverse possession under a recorded assurance of title (color of title) is required; section 28-2-102 gives a defense when there is assurance of title and seven years' possession, covering the entire boundary described. (Tenn. Code Ann. 28-2-101 to 28-2-103, as described in Cumulus Broadcasting v. Shim (Tenn. 2007); source)
  • Section 28-2-103, which does not involve color of title, protects an adverse holder after seven years only as to the portion in actual possession. (Tenn. Code Ann. 28-2-103, per Cumulus Broadcasting v. Shim; source)
  • Common-law adverse possession: uninterrupted, continuous possession for 20 years raises a presumed grant or deed; color or assurance of title is not required. (Cumulus Broadcasting v. Shim (Tenn. 2007); source)
  • Possession must be exclusive, actual, adverse, continuous, open and notorious for the required period. (Cumulus Broadcasting v. Shim; Tenn. Supreme Court press release, 7/31/2024; source)
  • Tax payment: 28-2-110(a) bars any action to recover real estate by a claimant who and whose predecessors failed to have it assessed and pay state and county taxes for more than 20 years. (Tenn. Code Ann. 28-2-110(a), quoted in Cumulus Broadcasting v. Shim; source)
  • Landlord detainer types: forcible entry and detainer (29-18-102), forcible detainer (29-18-103), unlawful detainer (29-18-104). (TN Courts, Landlord Tenant Update presentation; source)

Tennessee Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights: Rules for Selling a Rental

  • Turn the Tennessee Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights offer down and you owe us nothing

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • URLTA (applies in counties that adopted it): five-day grace period for rent. (TN Courts, Landlord Tenant Update presentation (URLTA slide); source)
  • Outside URLTA counties, only four sections of 66-7-101 et seq. apply: 109 (termination of tenancy), 110 (tenants with disabilities), 111 (service and support animals), 112 (domestic abuse). (TN Courts, Landlord Tenant Update presentation; source)
  • Tenant domestic-abuse protections appear in 66-28-205 and 66-28-517 (URLTA) and 66-7-109 and 66-7-112 (non-URLTA). (TN Courts, Landlord Tenant Update presentation; source)
Selling in Tennessee?

Get My Cash Offer →

Which Tennessee counties follow the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act?

Only the larger counties follow it. The act, found in Title 66, Chapter 28 of the Tennessee Code, reaches counties with more than 75,000 residents by the 2010 federal census. A Tennessee Courts presentation on residential evictions names nineteen: Shelby, Davidson, Knox, Hamilton, Rutherford, Williamson, Montgomery, Sumner, Wilson, Blount, Sullivan, Washington, Bradley, Sevier, Madison, Maury, Anderson, Greene and Putnam.

The remaining counties fall under Title 66, Chapter 7 of the Code, starting at section 101. The presentation says only four sections of that older law actually apply: section 109 on termination of tenancy, 110 on tenants with disabilities, 111 on service and support animals, and 112 on domestic abuse.

How the two Tennessee landlord tenant regimes differ. Source: Tennessee Courts residential evictions presentation.
TopicURLTA countiesAll other counties
Governing lawTitle 66, Chapter 28Title 66, Chapter 7 (four sections apply)
Rent grace periodFive days, not counting Sundays and legal holidaysNot addressed by the four applicable sections
Late fee cap10 percent of the rent past dueNot addressed by the four applicable sections
Notice types14 day, 7 day for repeat violations, 3 day14 day, 30 day, 3 day

Check which column your rental belongs in before you send any notice or promise any date. The county clerk or a local attorney can confirm it, and the answer changes what a notice must say.

What written notices does a Tennessee landlord send?

In a URLTA county, a landlord facing a material breach can deliver written notice that the lease ends after 14 days unless the tenant cures the problem. A repeat of substantially the same act or omission inside six months permits a seven day written notice. Section 66-28-505 sets out these steps, and the Tennessee Courts presentation adds a three day notice for violence, threats and unsanitary conditions.

  • Monthly tenancy: either party ends it by written notice delivered at least 30 days before the rent due date the notice specifies (section 66-28-512).
  • Weekly tenancy: written notice delivered at least ten days before the end date.
  • Tenant repairs to cure a breach need a written request from the tenant and written authorization from the landlord before work begins.
  • A holdover who remains without consent once the term ends is open to a suit for possession, back rent and reasonable attorney fees.

The presentation stresses that the owner must rely on the reasons stated in the notice when the case reaches court. New misconduct after a notice goes out calls for another notice. Subsidized housing requires written notice, and federal rules may differ from state law.

What happens to a lease if the landlord sells the house?

The statute addresses the seller's liability and says nothing that ends a tenancy. Section 66-28-305 releases a landlord who conveys to a bona fide purchaser in good faith from liability for later events, once the tenant has written notice of the conveyance and the security deposit has moved to the purchaser. Skip either step and the seller stays exposed.

Section 66-28-302 obliges a landlord to give the tenant who manages the property and who may receive service and notices for the owner, with an address for each. The same section makes that duty enforceable against any successor landlord, owner or manager, so whoever buys a rented house takes on that duty.

  • Tell the tenant in writing that the property changed hands and where the deposit now sits.
  • Hand over to the buyer the lease, the deposit and the tenant's contact details.
  • Ask the county clerk, a local attorney or the detainer court what notice your lease and county require before assuming the sale lets you end the lease.

Showings come with limits. Section 66-28-403 says a tenant should not unreasonably refuse entry so the landlord can exhibit the unit to actual or prospective buyers, while barring abuse of that access. The same section lists the only situations in which a landlord may enter without consent, such as an emergency or a court order.

How does Tennessee treat security deposits?

Section 66-28-301 requires URLTA-county landlords to place each deposit in an account used only for deposits, at a bank or lender regulated by Tennessee or the federal government. Tenants learn where the account is when they sign and pay, though the account number stays private.

  • Tenants may inspect the unit for the damage behind any charge, and the landlord may invite them to attend.
  • A landlord who skipped the separate account or the written damage listing may not keep any of the deposit.
  • Damage found later is recoverable only if the landlord spotted it inside 30 days after the tenant left or inside seven days after a new tenant took possession, whichever ends first.
  • When nothing is owed and a refund is due, the landlord sends a refund notice to the tenant's last known address, and if no reply arrives within 60 days the landlord may take the money out of the account.

A seller has to pass the deposit to the buyer to earn the release described above. Put the amount in the closing paperwork so both sides agree on it.

How does a Tennessee eviction case move through court?

A landlord files a detainer warrant in general sessions court. The presentation lists three types: forcible entry and detainer under section 29-18-102, forcible detainer under 29-18-103 and unlawful detainer under 29-18-104.

  • Service: the summons can go to any adult found in possession, or to a party named in the lease. Personal service supports a money judgment.
  • Posting: after three attempts on three different dates, documented on the warrant, service can be made by posting a copy on the door and mailing one, at least six days before the hearing. Posting supports possession only, not a money judgment.
  • Continuances: the maximum is 15 days unless the parties agree, the landlord consents, or no court is being held.
  • Appeal: a defendant has ten days to appeal to circuit court and must post bond. A certiorari route to circuit court runs 30 days and needs a meritorious reason and bond.
  • Writ of possession: when the landlord wins, the writ is executed and the landlord restored to possession immediately.

If a defendant appeals without posting the required bond, the landlord does not have to post one to obtain possession. The landlord is also entitled to interest on the judgment from the judgment date if the defendant's appeal fails.

What protections apply to domestic abuse victims in a rental?

The URLTA and the older law use identical wording, in sections 66-28-205 and 66-28-517 for URLTA counties and 66-7-109 and 66-7-112 elsewhere. If domestic abuse is the reason a tenancy could be ended, only the perpetrator may be evicted. The landlord may not evict the victim, minor children or innocent occupants, and the perpetrator stays financially liable.

A landlord may remove the perpetrator from the lease and have the remaining adult tenants qualify for a new agreement. The victim and the other adult tenants must agree in writing not to let the perpetrator return. A tenant who is a domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking victim can also request release from the lease by written notice, with a release date agreed within 30 days and a copy of either a valid order of protection after a hearing or documents showing a criminal charge.

A seller whose tenancy involves an order of protection should get legal advice before serving any notice.

More questions about Tennessee Landlord Tenant Law and Tenant Rights

Does the URLTA apply in my Tennessee county?

It applies in counties with more than 75,000 residents under the 2010 census. The Tennessee Courts presentation lists 19, including Davidson, Shelby, Knox, Hamilton and Rutherford. If your county is not listed, the shorter Title 66, Chapter 7 law applies, so confirm with your county clerk before sending notices.

How much notice ends a monthly rental?

In URLTA counties, section 66-28-512 asks for written notice at least 30 days before the rent due date the notice names. A weekly rental needs ten days. For other counties the courts presentation lists 14, 30 and three day notices, so match the notice to your situation.

Can a Tennessee landlord charge a late fee?

In URLTA counties, yes, a fee of up to a tenth of the rent past due, and only after the five day grace period. The grace period does not count Sundays or legal holidays. The presentation lists no late fee cap for other counties, so check your lease.

Does selling the house cancel the tenant's lease?

No statute says so. Section 66-28-305 only frees a seller from later liability after the tenant gets written notice and the deposit goes to the buyer. A local attorney or the clerk can tell you what notice your county expects before you end a lease.

How long does a Tennessee eviction take?

The statutes set no single timeline. Posted service must happen at least six days before the hearing, continuances are limited to 15 days, and a tenant has ten days to appeal. If the tenant appeals without bond, the landlord can still obtain possession.

Tennessee Eviction Notice Rules: Notice Types, Days and Selling the House

Cash Home Buyers in Tennessee
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Tennessee Eviction Notice Rules sale
  • Turn the Tennessee Eviction Notice Rules offer down and you owe us nothing

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • URLTA notice periods listed: fourteen-day, seven-day (repeat violations), three-day (violence, threats, unsanitary conditions); waiver of notice for nonpayment is possible. (TN Courts, Landlord Tenant Update presentation; source)
  • When judgment is for the plaintiff and a writ of possession is awarded, it is executed and the plaintiff restored to possession immediately. (Tenn. Code Ann. 29-18 (writ of possession), per TN Courts presentation; source)
  • Service: personal service on an adult in possession, or after three attempts on different dates, posting plus mailing at least six days before the hearing. (Tenn. Code Ann. 29-18-115 (shown as 29-18-15 in slide), per TN Courts presentation; source)
  • Continuance maximum 15 days unless parties agree, landlord consents or no court is held; defendant appeal within 10 days (29-18-129); certiorari to circuit court within 30 days. (Tenn. Code Ann. 29-18-118, 29-18-129, per TN Courts presentation; source)
Selling in Tennessee?
We buy Tennessee houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Which eviction notice does a Tennessee landlord have to give?

It depends on the county and the reason. Tennessee Courts judicial academy materials on landlord tenant evictions split the state into counties under the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (URLTA) and every other county, which falls under Tennessee Code Annotated 66-7-101 and following.

Where the rental sitsNotices listed
URLTA countyFourteen day, seven day for repeat violations, three day for violence, threats or unsanitary conditions
Any other county14 day, 30 day, 3 day

Source: Tennessee Courts judicial academy presentation. The slides also note that a waiver of notice for nonpayment is possible in URLTA counties, so read the lease before drafting the notice.

Which Tennessee counties follow the URLTA?

The same presentation lists nineteen counties: Anderson, Blount, Bradley, Davidson, Greene, Hamilton, Knox, Madison, Maury, Montgomery, Putnam, Rutherford, Sevier, Shelby, Sullivan, Sumner, Washington, Williamson and Wilson. A rental in Nashville, Memphis, Knoxville or Chattanooga lands in a URLTA county. A rental in a county outside that list uses the shorter set of rules in Title 66, Chapter 7.

In non-URLTA counties the presentation says only four statutes actually apply: Section 109 on termination of tenancy, Section 110 on tenants with disabilities, Section 111 on service and support animals, and Section 112 on domestic abuse. Ask the clerk of the general sessions court in your county to confirm which set of rules applies before you serve a notice.

What extra rules apply to rent in a URLTA county?

URLTA gives tenants a five day grace period, and Sundays and legal holidays do not count toward it. The maximum late fee is 10 percent. The act also covers security deposits, abandonment, essential services and the duties of both landlord and tenant.

  • Fourteen day notice, the first period the presentation lists.
  • Seven day notice for repeat violations.
  • Three day notice for violence, threats or unsanitary conditions.

A landlord who plans to sell an occupied rental should count the grace period before announcing a default, and should put the reason for the notice in writing, since the court holds the owner to the reasons stated.

How does a detainer warrant move through general sessions court?

Eviction starts with a detainer warrant filed in general sessions court. The presentation lists three types under Tennessee Code Annotated: forcible entry and detainer (29-18-102), forcible detainer (29-18-103) and unlawful detainer (29-18-104). The written notice matters in court, because the owner must rely on the reasons in the notice, and new misconduct after the notice calls for another notice.

Service rules shape what the judge can award. Personal service supports a money judgment. Service on an adult found in possession, service on a contractually named party, or posting can support possession only. For posting, the officer must attempt personal service on three different dates, record the attempts on the warrant, post a copy on the door and mail it, with the posting at least six days before the hearing.

How long can the hearing be delayed and when can the tenant appeal?

A continuance is capped at 15 days unless the parties agree, the landlord consents or no court is being held. After judgment, a defendant may appeal within ten days under 29-18-129, giving bond, or seek certiorari and supersedeas in circuit court within thirty days. The certiorari route requires a meritorious reason and a bond covering costs, damages and the rent for the premises during the litigation.

  • When judgment goes to the plaintiff and a writ of possession is awarded, it is executed and the plaintiff restored to possession immediately.
  • If the defendant appeals without posting the bond for one year of rent, the landlord does not have to post a bond to obtain possession.
  • When a defendant appeals and does post, the landlord's bond must be double the value of one year's rent.

A landlord also earns interest on the judgment from the date of judgment if the tenant's appeal fails.

What if the tenant cannot be found to serve?

The slides describe an "absent" defendant route. Personal service is dispensed with when the defendant is a nonresident, cannot be found and is believed to have left the state, the summons came back "not to be found in my county," the defendant's name or residence is unknown after diligent inquiry, or a domestic corporation has ceased doing business.

In those cases service by publication under Sections 21-1-203 through 21-1-205 applies, and the plaintiff must also post a copy of the publication notice on the front door or other front portion of the premises at least fifteen days before the date set for the defendant to appear. Keep a written record of each attempt to find the person.

What changes when the tenant is in subsidized housing or a domestic abuse survivor?

Subsidized leases bring in a third party. The presentation names HUD, THDA and Rural Development as sources, describes a three way agreement among landlord, HUD and tenant, and says the lease may not contradict the tenancy addendum. Notice requirements for a subsidized unit can differ from state law, so the owner needs written notice that fits both sets of rules.

Domestic abuse has its own protections in both URLTA and non-URLTA counties. If domestic abuse is the underlying offense for ending a tenancy, only the perpetrator may be evicted, and victims, minor children and innocent occupants may not be. A tenant who is a domestic abuse, sexual assault or stalking victim can ask in writing for release from the lease, with a release date agreed within 30 days and a copy of a valid order of protection or documents of a criminal charge.

What should a landlord check before filing a detainer warrant?

Run through the points below in order. Each comes from the court presentation and affects whether a judge can grant possession.

  • Confirm whether the county follows the URLTA or Title 66, Chapter 7.
  • Match the notice type and number of days to the reason for ending the tenancy.
  • Count the five day grace period for rent in a URLTA county, skipping Sundays and legal holidays.
  • Serve the warrant on an adult found in possession or on a named party to the lease, or document three attempts on different dates before posting.
  • Calendar the 15 day continuance limit, the ten day appeal period and the thirty day certiorari period.

A landlord who is also trying to sell should share this calendar with the buyer's agent so everyone plans around the same dates.

How does an eviction affect selling a Tennessee rental house?

An open detainer case, a recent notice and a tenant who may appeal all affect timing. A buyer who is financing may need vacant possession by closing, while an investor may accept the house with the tenant in place. The presentation says a writ of possession is what restores the plaintiff to possession, and a defendant has ten days to appeal, so a sale contract that depends on vacancy needs a closing date that leaves room for both steps.

Bring the lease, every notice, the detainer warrant and the judgment to your title company or closing attorney. Ask the general sessions clerk in the county for the case status before you accept a closing date.

More questions about Tennessee Eviction Notice Rules

How many days of notice must a Tennessee landlord give?

It depends on the county and the reason. The Tennessee Courts presentation lists fourteen, seven and three day notices in URLTA counties, and 14, 30 and 3 day notices elsewhere. Check the lease and the notice type for your county.

Which Tennessee counties follow the URLTA?

The judicial academy slides list nineteen: Anderson, Blount, Bradley, Davidson, Greene, Hamilton, Knox, Madison, Maury, Montgomery, Putnam, Rutherford, Sevier, Shelby, Sullivan, Sumner, Washington, Williamson and Wilson.

Does the tenant get a grace period?

In URLTA counties, yes. Tenants have five days, and Sundays and legal holidays do not count. The maximum late fee is 10 percent.

How fast can a landlord regain possession after winning?

Immediately once a writ of possession is awarded and executed. The defendant can still appeal within ten days or seek certiorari within thirty days, and the bond rules decide whether the landlord must wait.

Can a landlord evict a domestic abuse victim?

No, when domestic abuse is the underlying offense. Only the perpetrator may be evicted, and the landlord may not evict victims, minor children or innocent occupants.

title: Tennessee Probate Laws: Who Inherits, Small Estates and Selling the House
content:
Tennessee Probate Laws: Who Inherits, Small Estates and Selling the House

Cash Home Buyers in Tennessee
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Tennessee Probate Laws: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Tennessee Probate Laws sale
  • Turn the Tennessee Probate Laws offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Tennessee House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • A Small Estate (Small Estates Act, T.C.A. 30-4-101 to 30-4-105) means personal property not exceeding $50,000; it cannot transfer title to real estate. (Hawkins County Chancery Court, Small Estates Act Affidavit instructions; source)
  • A small estate cannot be opened until 45 days from date of death; affidavit filed with court with death certificate; original will, if any, deposited with clerk. (Hawkins County Chancery Court, Small Estates Act Affidavit instructions; source)
  • Intestate spouse share: if there are surviving issue, either one-third or a child's share (search/guide excerpt); any part of an estate not disposed of by will passes to heirs in the same manner. (Tennessee Probate Guide (TN Courts), general rules of descent; source)
  • If there is no surviving issue or parent, the estate goes to brothers and sisters and their issue by representation. (Tennessee Probate Guide (TN Courts); source)
Selling in Tennessee?
We buy Tennessee houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Which Tennessee court handles an estate?

The court that exercises probate jurisdiction in the county where the person lived at death handles the estate. Tennessee statutes call this simply the court, and they define it by the decedent's legal residence on the date of death. The clerk of that county's court is the first call.

The first practical question for a family holding an inherited house is whether anyone has been appointed to act for the estate. Letters from that court show who is authorized to act for the estate, and limited letters name only the property listed in the petition. A buyer or title company may ask what authority you hold before closing.

What is a small estate in Tennessee?

A small estate is a probate estate whose property does not exceed $50,000. The Small Estate Probate Act, Tennessee Code Title 30, Chapter 4, lets one or more competent adult heirs ask for limited letters instead of opening a full administration. The 2023 rewrite of the act passed the House 90 to 0 on March 16, 2023.

  • Waiting period: a petition can be filed after 45 days from the date of death, shown by the death certificate, if no one has filed a petition to appoint a personal representative in that time. The court can waive the wait for good cause.
  • Petition: a sworn petition lists each item of property, its value, each creditor and the amount owed.
  • Bond: a corporate surety bond equal to the property value is required, unless the petitioners are the sole heirs or sole beneficiaries, or all adult heirs and beneficiaries consent in writing.
  • Creditors: no notice to creditors is published, and creditors may not file claims in the small estate.
  • Closing: the limited letters stay open until the first anniversary of issuance, when the court automatically discharges the personal representative and surety.

A will can be used too. If the decedent left a will that distributes differently than intestacy would, the named personal representative may file it as a muniment of title, or record the original with the clerk along with witness affidavits, or two disinterested persons' affidavits for a handwritten will.

Can a small estate petition cover the house?

It cannot. The act defines property as personal property only, and the model limited letters state that no real property is at issue and that the letters give the personal representative no authority over real estate. A house or land therefore needs a different route.

If extra assets turn up that push the estate over $50,000, the court may allow the small estate to be converted to a full probate administration on a verified petition filed by the personal representative or a creditor. The people who received property earlier remain liable for what they were paid.

For an heir who wants to sell the home, the clerk of the probate court is the right place to ask what documents show authority over the deed. Bring the death certificate, any will, and a list of everyone who may have an interest in the property.

What can the holder of small estate letters do with the property?

The personal representative collects and preserves the assets listed in the petition, removes personal property from a unit the decedent leased, and cancels insurance that no longer applies after the death. Anyone who owes the estate money, or holds estate property such as a bank, must pay or deliver it once shown a clerk-certified copy of the limited letters and receiving a demand. A person who hands property over in good faith is released from further liability to the estate and its creditors.

If a holder refuses, the property can be recovered, and a court can compel delivery, with costs charged to the person who wrongfully refused. Distribution then goes to the heirs as the law provides, or under the will if it was admitted as a muniment of title or recorded with the clerk. Those limits are worth knowing before an heir spends money on the house, because small estate letters reach vehicles, accounts and similar personal property, while the deed stays outside them.

What does full administration of an estate involve?

Full administration starts with letters testamentary if there is a will, or letters of administration if there is none. The steps below come from the General Assembly's bill summary of present law.

  • Inventory: within 60 days after taking office, the personal representative must complete an accurate inventory of the probate estate and return it to the clerk, verified under oath.
  • Beneficiary notice: within the same 60 days, each legatee or devisee gets a copy of the will or the relevant paragraphs, and each residuary distributee of an intestate estate gets a copy of the letters of administration.
  • Notice to creditors: within 30 days after letters are issued, the clerk publishes two consecutive weekly notices in a county newspaper, or posts written notices in three public places if the county has no newspaper.
  • Claims: creditors must file by the earlier of the dates in the notice, which includes 12 months from the date of death, or their claims are forever barred.
  • Exceptions: until 30 days after four months from the notice, the personal representative or an interested party may except to a claim in writing.

Those periods mean a house can sit in an estate for most of a year. Ask the clerk which dates apply to your file, because the notice sets them. A seller who wants speed has to work within them rather than around them.

How do small estate and full administration compare?

The comparison below shows what changes when a probate estate is under $50,000 and contains no real property. If the estate holds a house, the right column is the one that applies.

Small estate procedure and full administration in Tennessee. Sources: 2023 small estate bill text and the General Assembly's summary of present law on notice and inventory.
FeatureSmall estateFull administration
Value limit$50,000 or lessNo limit
Real propertyNot coveredNot limited to personal property
Wait to file45 days after death, unless the court waives itTiming follows the appointment and the notice dates
Notice to creditorsNone publishedTwo weekly notices in a county newspaper
Claims barCreditors may not fileEarlier of the notice dates or 12 months from death
Court involvementLimited letters, open about one yearInventory and notices to the clerk

What debts can follow an inherited house?

Medical assistance is one debt that can reach beyond the estate. The small estate statute says that if property is distributed before all medical assistance owed to TennCare under Tennessee Code section 71-5-116 is paid, both the personal representative and the person receiving the property stay liable to TennCare, up to the value received. Anyone who plans to sell inherited property should ask the clerk or an attorney whether a TennCare claim exists before sharing proceeds.

Other debts matter too. Those who receive property from a small estate remain liable for up to one year after receiving it to unpaid creditors, to anyone with a prior right to the property, and to any personal representative appointed later.

Property taxes continue while a house waits in probate. Our Tennessee property tax guide explains the bill, the appeal calendar and the relief programs, and the county trustee can give a current balance for the parcel.

More questions about Tennessee Probate Laws

How long does probate take in Tennessee?

The creditor claim period can run as long as 12 months from the date of death, which sets the pace of a full administration. A small estate stays open until the first anniversary of the limited letters. Ask the probate clerk for the dates in your own notice.

Can I sell an inherited house through the small estate procedure?

No. The small estate law covers personal property only, and the limited letters say they give no authority over real estate. A house needs another form of probate, so ask the clerk of the court in the county where the owner lived.

How soon can I file a small estate petition?

After 45 days from the date of death, as shown by a death certificate, unless someone has already filed to appoint a personal representative. The court may waive the 45 day wait for good cause shown.

Do creditors get notice in a small estate?

No. The statute says a notice to creditors must not be published and creditors are not permitted to file claims. Recipients of property still owe unpaid creditors for up to one year after receiving it.

What must a personal representative do within 60 days?

Complete and verify an inventory of the probate estate and return it to the clerk, and send beneficiaries a copy of the will or letters. The 60 days run from entering on the administration.

When property tax goes unpaid in Tennessee, the statutes allow the taxing authority to sell a lien or the property itself, and they give the owner a set time to redeem.

What the official sources say

  • Redemption: one year from entry of the order confirming the tax sale to the tax sale purchaser. (T.C.A. 67-5-2701(a)(1)(D), per TN Courts delinquent tax handout; source)
  • Redemption period can be shortened to 30 days if the purchaser shows the property is vacant and abandoned by 3 periodic inspections over two months at different times of day. (T.C.A. 67-5-2701(n), per TN Courts delinquent tax handout; source)
  • A redeeming taxpayer pays delinquent taxes, penalty, interest, court costs and interest on the purchase price at 1% per month, levied from the date of sale and on the first day of each month until 30 days after the motion to redeem is filed. (T.C.A. 67-5-2701(b); Tenn. Attorney General Opinion 15-22; source)
  • Motion for lawful charges must be filed within 30 days after mailing of the notice of redemption. (T.C.A. 67-5-2701(d), per TN Courts delinquent tax handout; source)
